newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks halt two-session slide; Nasdaq ends lower.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks halt two-session slide; Nasdaq ends lower.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks closed higher on Monday as a rebound in bonds halted a two-session slide that temporarily pushed the Dow Jones industrial average below 8,000 points.
The Dow gained 30.89 points to 8,062.11 after retreating earlier to 7,064.56. The blue-chip index had lost 228 points in the previous two sessions as long-term interest rates soared unexpectedly.
In the broader market, declining issues still led advances 1,483 to 1,344 on moderate volume of 480 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

The late-session recovery in the blue-chip stocks did not spread fully across all sectors, with the Nasdaq composite index finishing off 11.78 points at 1,586.74 on further profit taking in the high-technology stocks.
Despite the mixed performance, traders said they did not see much of a carryover from Friday's 157-point Dow sell-off. Several said trading was typical of a summer Monday.
"We really didn't get much of a follow-through to that scare on Friday," said Bill Allyn, head of trading at Jefferies & Co. "That in itself is good news."

As they did last week, stocks keyed off bonds Monday. The rebound in blue chips was triggered after bonds responded to a news wire report that Federal Reserve Governor Susan Phillps suggested that there was no immediate need for a credit tightening.
Recent economic data that pointed to a strengthening economy have rekindled market speculation that the Fed will need to raise interest rates to keep inflation at bay.
The Federal Open Market Committee -- the central bank's policy-setting body -- meets Aug. 19 to decide on the direction of interest rates.
In the bond market, the yield on the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury closed at Friday's 6.64 percent after falling late in the day from 6.69 percent, the highest since July 2.
Traders said they expected tentative trading until Wednesday's report on retail sales and July wholesale inflation. Thursday brings a report on retail inflation.

July retail sales data, due Wednesday, were forecast to rise 0.7 percent after a 0.5 percent gain in June. The July producer price index is also set for release Wednesday and the consumer price index is due Thursday.
Investors are looking for any hints in the data of inflationary pressures in the economy.
"Don't expect it to get much clearer until Wednesday and Thursday," said Guy Truicko, equity portfolio manager at Unity Management. "Then we'll see where we go from there."

Financial stocks, which are sensitive to shifts in interest rates, got a lift from bonds. American Express Co. rose 1-12/16 to 82-3/16, J.P. Morgan & Co. rose 2-12/16 to 113-7/16 and Citicorp was up 2-1/4 to 136-1/4.

Pharmaceutical stocks slipped. Morgan Stanley lowered its opinion of the drug sector, saying recent increased industry spending reduced chances of near-term positive earnings surprises. Warner-Lambert Co. fell 3-7/8 to 132-1/4, Merck & Co. lost 3-9/16 to 95-1/4 and Eli Lilly & Co. dropped 4 to 108-11/16.
Hershey Foods Corp. rose 4-7/8 to 57-3/8, boosted by an upgrade from Morgan Stanley.

Publisher Reader's Digest Association Inc. was up 3-3/8 to 28-1/4 after saying its chairman and chief executive officer, James Schadt, had resigned. The move came one month after the company slashed its dividend and earnings forecast.

CSG Systems International Inc. rose 3-1/4 to 26-3/8 after it signed two major agreements with a Tele-Communications Inc. affiliate. Its rival, USCS International Inc., fell 10-7/8 to 20-1/8 on the news. Both firms offer customer management products and services.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 3.46 points to 937.00. The American Stock Exchange index was off 1.80 to 644.35.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 1.42 to 485.21. The average share was up 14 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 8,890.104, up 8.265, or 0.09 percent.
